chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl narrated from Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Zafarani from Hammad ibn Isa from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Aban ibn Abi Ayyash from Sulaym ibn Qays al-Hilali from Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) who said:
I heard him say much speech, then he said: 'And give them from all of that the share of the near kin.'
Allah the Exalted said: 'If you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down to Our servant on the day of the Criterion, the day when the two armies met.'

By Allah, the 'near kin' refers to us, and they are those whom Allah has joined to His own self and to His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). So He said: 'Then for Allah is its fifth, and for the Messenger and for the near kin and the orphans and the poor and the wayfarer.'
And He did not assign us a share in the portion of alms-giving (zakat); Allah honored His Prophet and honored us so that He would not feed us with the dregs of people's hands.

key_terms.أَوْسَاخَ أَيْدِي النَّاسِ: Dregs of people's hands (metaphor for common people's hands)
key_terms.ذِي الْقُرْبَى: Near kin (specifically Ahl al-Bayt in this context)
key_terms.يَوْمَ الْفُرْقَانِ: Day of the Criterion (Battle of Badr)

ai.seo_question: Who are the 'near kin' entitled to Khums according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) clarifies that the 'Dhi al-Qurba' in Surah Al-Anfal (8:41) specifically denotes the Ahl al-Bayt, distinguishing their exclusive right to the Prophet's portion of Khums from the general populace. He further explains that while they receive Khums, they were excluded from the share of Zakat (alms) to preserve their dignity and avoid being sustained by the contributions of the common people, a distinction rooted in their unique spiritual status.
